Objectives:
The purpose of the Proposed Action is to reduce hazardous fuels on BLM land in Antelope
Valley. Many of the areas proposed for treatment are immediately adjacent to homes and
communities in Antelope Valley. In these cases, the proposed treatments are intended to
decrease the intensity of future wildland fires in the treated areas, and increase the safety of
residents, private property, and firefighters working to protect the community and suppress
fires.
Planned_Implementation:
Work includes standing dead, dead and down, and standing live pinyon pine. All slash must be treated. Firewood-sized material will be yarded, piled and left for public gathering at BLM-designated sites within each unit.

Work Sequence - Cutting, yarding, slash treatment, and site restoration shall be performed in an organized and
systematic manner, as determined in the pre-work conference. To minimize fire hazard, slash work must be conducted
simultaneously or progressively with tree felling and yarding operations. For these Items, slash treatment is chipping.
The nature of this work will result in some ground disturbance, however the Contractor is expected to conduct all
operations with professionalism and care to ensure soil and vegetation disturbance and displacement are the minimum
practicable for the designated tasks.

Cutting (Specifications Common to All Pinyon Units - Live pinyon pine exceeding 1 foot in total height shall be cut to
achieve individual unit specifications listed below. No live branches shall be left on the stump of cut trees. Stump
height shall conform to Stump Height in Section 6.13.1 in this contract. All standing dead pinyon pine shall be cut.
Dead and down pinyon pine shall be bucked and treated as firewood or slash. In all units, areas will be left uncut. The
uncut areas shall range from just a few trees in a small group, to patches of trees up to 1/2 acre in size. Average
size shall be approximately 1/4 acre. Groups or patches of larger-sized individual trees shall be sought out by the ! Contractor for retention as uncut areas. Groups or patches should be located more or Jess randomly throughout the
N units, as conditions permit. While creation of very large openings should be avoided, a strict spacing pattern should also
not be used in locating groups or patches. No groups or patches of pinyon pine shall be located within 75 feet of the unit
boundaries. Groups or patches of pinyon pine shall be located at least 75 feet from other groups or patches. Standing
dead or dead and down trees located within the uncut groups or patches shall be cut and treated. The Contracting
Officer's Rep. will work closely with the Contractor in the initial stages to answer questions and ensure these
specifications are clearly understood.

ITEM 0002AA (Dump) Specifications: Leave approximately 42 groups or patches of uncut pinyon pine (40 north of
old dump site, 2 south of old dump site).
ITEM 0002AB (Clinic) Specifications: Leave approximately 23 groups or patches of uncut pinyon pine.
ITEM 0002AC (Patricia) Specifications: Leave approximately 14 groups or patches of uncut pinyon pine.
ITEM 0002AD (Camp) Specifications: Leave approximately 24 groups or patches of uncut pinyon pine.
ITEM 0002AE (Birchim Flat Rd.) Specifications: Leave approximately 12 groups or patches of uncut pinyon pine.

Yarding (Specifications Common to All Pinyon Units) - All firewood-sized material (4" diameter and larger) shall be
brought to ELM-designated sites for piling, so as to be available to the general public as firewood. All piling shall be
done on BLM land, within the project boundaries. No skidding is allowed. Material must be transported from stump to
landing fully off the surface of the ground. Material may be brought to the landing by non-motorized means. Motorized
equipment may also be used. If motorized equipment is used, the equipment&$s size must be approximately equal to that
of an ATV and small trailer. Regardless of yarding method used, soil displacement is minimal, and residual vegetation
is protected to the greatest extent practicable.

Mitigation to replace the vegetation and to reduce erosion will be
both natural and artificial. All the native species are adapted to fire.
Some sprout from the root crown, some have seeds which need the heat of

burn area and fertilization of potential permanent conversions to
increase the density of ground cover and, thus, decrease the severity
of erosion.

overstory of sagebrush, which should allow native species to be more competitive with
invasive plants. The brush beating is done in multiple strips ranging from 40-50 feet wide,
with each strip separated by 50-70 feet of vegetation that has not been manipulated. The
brush was also manipulated for 50 feet on either side of roads within these grazing units

Blackpoint Unit- abundant new growth sage; bunch grasses are present with a high volume of cured cheat grass. This west side of the project is a high threat to the project and any fire into this area will burn readily. The untreated strips would not sustain fire spread without additional fine fuels.  As of 2007, the community of Eureka/Diamond Valley was determined to be at moderate risk of loss from a wildfire on public lands.

Objectives:
•Reduce pinyon, juniper and sagebrush cover on sagebrush and mountain shrub ecological sites in order to (1) improve the overall vegetative composition within the ecological site potential; (2) promote the recovery and establishment of perennial grass and forb species; (3) improve the health, vigor and production of antelope bitterbrush communities and (4) improve the age-class distribution of even-aged sagebrush stands
• Improve the available habitat for neighboring sage grouse, mule deer and elk populations
• Reduce the risk of large catastrophic wild fires by reducing fuel loading and continuity within the North Spring Valley Watershed and meet FRCC I
• Restore the historic disturbance regime within the project area
Planned_Implementation: Mechanical treatments such as mowing or hand cutting in areas containing insufficient levels of understory fuels, young pinyon and juniper establishment and decadent, even-aged stands of sagebrush.  Mowing would be conducted with a brush mower pulled by a rubber-wheeled tractor.  Mowing or other mechanical treatments would be conducted in a mosaic fashion by\r\nmowing strips and incorporating irregular (not straight) boundary lines.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Throughout the burned area, soils are inherently prone to runoff generation. Because the fire consumed soil organic matter and coarse debris in most parts of the burn, the potential for runoff generation from a given precipitation event has increased. Decreases in vegetation/debris/litter cover, increases in runoff generation, and decreases in soil structure and cohesion (due to loss of organic matter) have also increased the susceptibility of soils to erosion from sheet flow. On steeper slopes, there is also increased risk of rill erosion. Reestablishing vegetative cover and placement of stabilization structures
would reduce the effects of erosion.
   Buckskin Mountain is winter range for the Paunsaugunt and Kaibab deer herds. The Paunsaugunt Habitat Management Plan approved in May, 1984, identified the area as critical winter range. Browse species are an important source of forage for deer during this period. Grass and forb species are important forage species in early spring. Stabilizing the burned area would help preserve these deer herds.
   Covering seed using mechanical methods may negatively impact cultural sites. Identifying and avoiding these sites prior to
treatment would minimize these impacts.
   The pre-burn vegetation of the Buckskin Fire was a mix of pinyon-juniper woodland and sagebrush grassland communities. Stabilization actions would prevent the establishment and/or spread of noxious and invasive non-native species, especially cheatgrass.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Wire Pass Fire resulted in a 1,503 acres of Critical Winter Mule Deer Habitat burned. The
Paunsagaunt Deer Management Unit is a trophy mule deer unit within the area that was burned.
This unit is an important winter deer area for most of the mule deer herds within southern Utah and
is considered the longest migration route of mule deer in Utah.
The Wire Pass Fire did burn approximately 15 acres within the Paria River Wilderness Area. The fire
affected the Mollies Nipple grazing allotment. Current BLM policy requires that the burn areas be
protected from livestock grazing to allow for establishment of vegetation on the site.
Based on these findings, past fire history in similar areas, and visits to the burned area, protecting
the watershed values and reducing the erosion potential would be a priority for the Wire Pass ESR
project. Additionally, containment and control of invasive, non-native annual grasses such as
cheatgrass, which may exacerbate erosion potential and fire frequency and severity that would
further degrade crucial mule deer habitat is also a very high priority.

Other Special Status Species that could occur in the area might be burrowing owl, ferruginous hawk, and Swainson&$s hawk. Ferruginous hawk occur yearlong and utilize sagebrush-grass communities for foraging habitat. Swainson&$s hawk uses sagebrush-grass communities for foraging habitat as well and occurs during spring, summer, and fall. Burrowing owls mostly utilize grassland habitat for nesting and foraging during spring, summer, and fall.
3.   Cultural Resources could be exposed by the elimination of vegetative cover and increased erosion.
4.   Noxious and invasive non-native species, especially cheatgrass are prone to invade pinyon-juniper woodland and sagebrush grassland communities after fire.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Soil/water stabilization- The vast areas of exposed soils of the burn area are without protective vegetation.  Wind and water erosion will continue if left unprotected. The path of the Dog Valley Fire, as it crossed the 15 Interstate, was nearly four (4) miles wide. The freeway is located in a series of canyons, such as Dog Valley with mountains on each side. The BLM lands are generally to the
west and Forest Service lands to the east. Runoff from the mountains into the canyons could cause severe flooding across the 1-15 Interstate. Canyon winds could cause dust storms along the freeway making visibility limited, causing unsafe driving conditions.

Wildlife- The area around the burn provides habitat for many small rodents, birds and reptiles.  Bald eagles, ferruginous hawks and burrowing owls depend on the area for foraging habitat.  Loss of vegetation for habitat could impact these species.

Critical Heritage Resources- Critical heritage resources such as historical or cultural artifacts may be located on the burn area. With the loss of vegetation that has been covering the different resources, protection
would be impossible. Completion of ground seeding efforts could also damage these resources if not identified and flagged.

Invasive plants- The entire area burned by the Dog Valley Fire has been dominated by Scotch thistle.
Ground seeding operations must be completed prior to the emergence of Scotch thistle and cheatgrass this fall or in early spring. In the event this plan is not approved, the burn area could become totally re-infested by Scotch thistle and cheatgrass.

Objectives: Apply and cover seed to the ground of the burned area prior to the winter and spring storms to establish seeded species.
Planned_Implementation: It is proposed to aerial seed l l,520 acres and single chain 10,075 acres on the Dog Valley Fire located T. 24 & 25 S., R. 6, 7 & 8 W. two (2) miles northwest of Cove Fort, Millard County, Utah. The aerial seeding and single chaining will begin as soon as the funds are made available this fall (October) or early in the spring of 2007 (March). Approximately 11,520 acres will be aerial seeded prior lo the single chaining operations. A fixed wing plane will be used that will have a load capacity of 800 lbs. or more. The seeding rate will be 12.7 pounds per acre. The aerial seeding project will be done by contract and only a certified pilot will fly the plane. Fueling area and landing strips will be the responsibility of the contractor. A certified COR/PI BLM employee will monitor the seeding operations and make changes when necessary. At no time will the BLM flag for the plane or allow the plane in the air when conditions are unsafe.
Actual_Implementation: Approximately 11520 acers were aerial seeded and 10075 were single chained in the fall/spring of 2006/2007.  Studies were established throughout the aerial seeded areas to evaluate the success of the seeding.  Use frequency studies were used to determine the success of the seeding.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: The aerial seeding studies show good success 36 seedlings of seeded species and 7.5% live cover.  The single chain studies show 68 seedlings and 5.25% live cover.  It appears the two treatments are doing well and we expect to reach our goal of 20% perennial cover. The average percent cover of perennial vegetation is 10.75% point data for the three treatment types. Individually the average percent ground cover from point data for aerial seed only is 13%, aerial seed and single chain is 10.5%, and ground seeding 10%. The average relative frequency of perennial vegetation for the three treatments is 66% and 49% average being seeded species. In the  project area remaining shrub lands are dominated by homogenous stands of mature sagebrush with declining, remnant populations of native perennial forbs and grasses. Trt_Concerns_Desc: The North Fremont Allotment presently has 3500 acres of treatable, decadent, Wyoming big sagebrush habitat. This habitat consists of a monoculture of 80 to 100 year old sagebrush that is lacking an understory of desirable perennial grasses and forbs. This allotment presently does not have sufficient vegetative diversity, cover, composition or forage, to provide for BLM&$s multiple use needs.\r\n\r\nThe proposed Dixie harrow treatment would improve the vegetative resource and therefore restore the rangeland. The decadent sagebrush stands, that are of little or no value to wintering big game, other wildlife species, livestock and watershed, would be treated in an effort to improve vegetative cover and composition. An increase in desirable, upland forage and a decrease in overland flow/soil erosion would occur.

Planned_Implementation:
A total of 3500 acres of decadent, Wyoming, big sagebrush rangeland would be double harrowed and broadcast seeded (see attached map). After the area is harrowed once, then a combination of broadcast seeding and harrowing would be used to complete the action. 

The harrowing would be done on the contour as much as possible. This is very important for the improvement of the watershed, because harrowing on the contour greatly reduces the amount of overland flow and soil movement during runoff periods. The harrow creates furrows and keeps maximum water on-site, therefore improving seedling establishment and survival.

A Dixie Harrow would be pulled behind a four-wheel drive tractor. A large, broadcast seeder that is tied into the tractor hydraulic system would be used to broadcast the seed.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The project involves double harrowing and broadcast seeding 3,000 acres of Wyoming big
sagebrush habitat. Eleven species would be used in the seed mix ( 4 forbs, 2 browse, 5 grasses):
Appar Lewis flax, Delar small burnet, yellow sweetclover, Eski sainfoin, forage kochia,
antelope bitterbrush, Covar sheep fescue, Luna pubescent wheatgrass, Hycrest crested
wheatgrass, Russian wildrye and Magnar great basin wildrye. After the area is harrowed once,
then a combination of broadcast seeding and harrowing would be used to complete the action.
The second harrowing would be done in the opposite direction of the first harrowing. This is
crucial to the success of the project, because it maximizes the kill of the decadent, nonproductive
sagebrush and it also finalizes the preparation of the seedbed. The harrowing would be done on
the contour as much as possible. This is very important for the improvement of the watershed,
because harrowing on the contour greatly reduces the amount of overland flow and soil
movement during runoff periods. It keeps maximum water on-site and improves seedling
establishment and survival.

Planned_Implementation:
A Dixie Harrow (43 feet wide; 12,000 lbs.) would be pulled behind a 450 horsepower, fourwheel
drive tractor, that has dual tires all around (8). A large, Herd broadcast seeder (Model
2440; 21 bushel capacity), that is tied into the tractor hydraulic system, would be used to
broadcast the seed.

Objectives: To improve forage conditions for deer and cattle.
Planned_Implementation: The area will be chained or plowed, depending on the cover, and seeded to Crested Wheatgrass. Certain areas will be left unchained to provide cover for the deer and shade for the cattle. If browse seed can be obtained from the Utah State Fish & Game Dept. it will also be planted.
Actual_Implementation:
The seed bed preparation started in the fall (9/22/66) but due to stormy we t conditions
work was hampered to the point that work was suspended in early December.
Most of the trees had been chained and windrowed and some of the area had been
plowed one time over. Kill was not too good. No seed was drilled at this time .
Work commenced again in the fall, 9/12/67. Work was completed October 25, 1967 .
Brush kill appears to be good in most places but only fair on some of the rocky
ridges. Soil conditions varied from dry to wet in the fall of 1967. Seeded
species was changed from crested wheatgrass  to Russian wild rye due to high cost
of crested wheatgrass. Seeded at 6 pounds per acre.
Total cost per acre $15.76 .

Objectives:
The object of this contract is to
reduce wildland fuel, improve wildlife habitat and improve landscape health by rollerchopping this
pinyon and juniper site.

OBJECTIVES
Based on vegetation mosaics identified within the Uncompahgre Fire Management Plan,
discussions with BLM resource specialists, fire managers, ecologists, and Colorado Division of
Wildlife habitat specialists the following objectives were developed for the Mailbox/Dry Park
Project.
1 )Reduce potential fire behavior and resistance to control within .25 miles of, and primarily
upwind from, the electric lines, gas lines, and private inholdings within the Mailbox/Dry Park
area by creating a somewhat linear mosaic dominated by 75% early and early-mid seral (grass,
forbs, and low shrubs) with 25% late-mid and late-old growth (decadent sage and dense
pinyon/juniper). The patch size in deer emphasis areas should be 5-50 acres. The patch size in
elk emphasis areas should be 50-200 acres. Primarily use mechanical treatments, followed by
prescribed burning, to reduce fuel loadings arid maintain earlier seral communities .. Complete
these treatments by March, 2007
2)Reduce potential fire behavior and resistance to control within .5 miles of private lands south
of Mailbox Park by creating a mosaic of vegetation types dominated by 75% early and early-mid
seral (grass/forb/shrub) with 25% late-mid and late-old growth (remnant sage and dense
pinyon/juniper). The patch size should be 5-50 acres due to deer emphasis in this area. Primarily
use mechanical treatments, followed by prescribed burning to reduce fuel loadings. and maintain
earlier seral communities. Complete these treatments by March, 2007.
3)Improve deer winter range throughout Mailbox Park by creating a mosaic of vegetation types.
40% of these areas should be early and early-mid seral (grass forb/shrub) with 60% late-mid and
late-old growth (remnant sage and dense pinyon/juniper). The patch size should be 5-50 acres
separated by 150-600 feet to preserve adequate cover. Work with private landowners to
incorporate private lands into treatments as able. Primarily use prescribed burning with limited
mechanical treatment. Implement these treatments from 2005 to 2012.
4)Improve elk winter range throughout Dry Park by creating a. mosaic of vegetation types. 40%
of this area should be early and early-mid seral (grass/forb/shrub) with 60% mid-late and late-old
growth (remnant sage and dense pinyon/juniper). The patch size should be 50-200 acres
separated by 1000-2000 feet to preserve adequate cover. Work with private landowners to
incorporate private lands into treatments as able. Primarily use prescribed burning with limited
mechanical treatment. Implement these treatments from 2005 to 2012.
5)By the fifth year following each treatment the canopy/ground cover should be as shown in
Table 1 for various vegetation types and treatment types (includes 'leave islands'). [Table 1 is in the Environmental Assessment Record] 
6)Improve watershed condition by improving ground cover over 50% of Mailbox/Dry Park by
100% by 2016.
7)Treatments will be designed, implemented, and re-seeded in a manner that will ensure that
there is no net increase in density or extent of noxious or invasive weeds within the treatment
areas.
Planned_Implementation:
The contractor will pull the roller chopper filled with water within areas for treatment. All roller
chopping will be done in a manner as instructed by the Pl/COR. That is, to roller chop in a
continuous manner.

The project will be accomplished by the contractor using the bulldozer to pull the rollerchopper
over the vegetation in the designated areas, and apply seed provided by the BLM. The pattern and
shape of treatment areas are shown in the attached map. Edges of the treatment shall be "flagged&&
by bright plastic surveying ribbon. Treatment areas are shown on the attached map. The areas will
be seeded while pulling the rollerchopper. At the direction of the Project Inspector (Pl) or
Contracting Officers Representative (COR) untreated areas or individual trees will be left scattered
throughout. Straight line edges will be avoided where possible. Untreated areas larger than 2 acres
in size will not be count as part of the acreage to be treated. The seeding rate will be 8 pounds per
acre.

Objectives:

- improve the habitat for Gunnison Sage Grouse by maintaining open sagebrush parks and attain vegetative standards for habitat identified within the conservation plan.
- Remove 85 to 95 % of the PJ that has encroached within the sagebrush parks through the treatment process.
- Improve the herbaceous cover within the sagebrush community by attaining a grass cover of 15 to 20 percent and a forb cover of 10 to 15 % in 10 years.
Planned_Implementation: The proposed action is to mechanically treat approximately 300 acres within a sagebrush park which is experiencing PJ encroachment in the Spring Creek area on the west end of Pinon Mesa at mid elevation. A rollerchopper would be used to remove the encroaching PJ as well as serve as a tool to provide an adequate seed bed for seeded species to improve the herbaceous cover within the sagebrush community.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Glade Park and Pinion Mesa in western Colorado support a population of Gunnison Sage Grouse. The Pinion Mesa Gunnison Sage Grouse Conservation Plan, prepared by BLM, Colorado Division of Wildlife, and private landowners, was approved in
May of 2000. This plan identified the loss of sagebrush habitat as the most threatening factor to the survival of sage grouse in this area. Pinon-Juniper (PJ) encroachment was one of the primary reasons leading to the loss of open sagebrush parks. Since the year 2000 several thousand acres both on BLM and private land has been treated to maintain open sagebrush parks with adequate herbaceous cover. Objectives:
----BAR/ES Plan----
Aerial seeding...to effectively apply the seed on 400 acres of the burn.

----EA----
It was recommended that native plants be seeded. Shrubs that would be planted would be high value wildlife browse plants (bitterbrush and mahogany), a variety of grasses and forbs. Both browse species tend not re-sprout following a fire and were probably killed during the fire. Yellow sweetclover, an introduced legume species should be added to the seed mix. The clover would serve as a short lived nurse crop and produce nitrogen to fertilize the other seeded plants. ----BAR/ES Plan---
Aerial seeding will be completed with contract aircraft. 

Application of the seed with this contract will be on 400 acres of public land on the upper portion of the burn in Emma Park.  

BLM will conduct a pre-work conference with the aircraft contractor and pilot to review the contract specifications and logistical layout of the project area.  BLM will provide maps and assist with flagging and flight line swath directions on the ground for proper seed application.  BLM may fly a reconnaissance flight with the contractor as part of the pre-work conference, if necessary.  BLM will deliver the seed to the contractor at the aircraft loading area.  Contractor will supply personal equipment, fuel and other materials associated with operation and maintenance of the aircraft.  The contractor will be responsible for loading the seed on the aircraft.

Contractor will have radio equipment capability to communicate with BLM ground crews for proper seed placement on the ground.  The aircraft, pilot and equipment will be certified by the Office of Aircraft and Safety (OAS).  Line of site and personal discretion will be utilized in conjunction with the BLM ground crews for proper application of the seed.  

Personal safety of the pilot and BLM staff will be ensured if the contract specifications are followed and good judgment is a top priority with all involved in the operation.  Every member of the operation has a personal responsibility for their own safety and the safety of the other party members. The BLM ground crew and the pilot will monitor conditions and
hazards at each phase of the operation to determine if operations should be stopped or modified to complete the project in a safe and efficient manner.

Visually inspect the flight lines of the aircraft, check number of seeds per square foot of coverage for the correct pounds per acre is being applied.  Track flight safety and assist the pilot with wind and flight operations from the project site.

The objective of this project is to increase the percentage of early and early-mid seral
stages (up to 30% of the area for early and 30% for early-mid) in the project area.
The proposed action is to reset vegetative
succession on a number of old chainings and plow and seedings scattered
across the landscape. This would improve vegetative diversity, composition,
and productivity of the landscape by creating a mosaic of different age
classes of vegetation. The increased diversity would benefit big game, small
mammal and bird species, that depend upon this variety; open grasslands,
sage brush communities, and mature pin on and juniper communities to
complete some phase of their life cycles.

This should reduce the potential for increased soil erosion.

Planned_Implementation:
Thinning will occur within 600 feet of the Northern Boundary for a total area of approximately 127 acres of
BLM land as measured by the contractor. Trees will be thinned by removing all trees (except Aspen) that are  greater than 6 .0 inches in diameter and
leaving a stump height of no more  than 6.0 inches. All thinning shall be done by a mechanical shearing machine and or by hand held portable
equipment (chainsaws). Limb branches of all residual trees to 7 feet in height. Slash from hand-thinned trees will be bucked to manageable lengths and piled in open areas for
future burning. All slash created from the above mentioned activities will be hand piled. Piles will
be located in open areas, out from underneath the crowns of residual trees as much as possible to
reduce crown scorch on remaining trees. Any tree deemed to be a hazard tree that is  greater than 6.0 inches
shall be removed.
All dead and down measuring 2.0 inches to 6.0 inches in diameter will be bucked and piled for
future burning. All dead and down that is greater than 6.0 inches up to 12.0 inches in diameter will be limbed and
bucked, into approximately 6 feet lengths and separated to allow for greater decomposition.
Cut all conifer and aspen snags (standing dead trees) that provide a safety concern, and treat standing
or hung-up dead from 2.0 to 12.0 inches in diameter into manageable sized lengths for piling. This
will include the branches and tops of large fallen snags.

Planned_Implementation:
Slash Treatment:
The term "slash" means all debris resulting from logging operations. Slash in this
provision is considered to be all woody vegetative material (including cull logs, chunks,
tops, limbs, branches, snags, damaged or destroyed reproduction, saplings, and uprooted
stumps) that is created or disturbed by any type of vegetative cutting, clearing,
construction, or silvicultural treatment.
Slash disposal shall be accomplished by machine piling, as described below. At the
Contracting Officer’s discretion, and with his prior approval, slash disposal may be
accomplished through the lopping and scattering of slash, or through a combination of
machine piling and lop and scatter (also described below). Regardless of treatment, the
top and side branches of all trees, that are cut or knocked down, and that are seven (7)
inches DBH or greater, shall be completely trimmed to a six (6) inch or less, top
diameter.
Regardless of treatment, the top and side branches of all live or dead, lodgepole pine,
that are cut or knocked down, and that are five (5)- and six (6)-inch diameter at breast height trees shall be
completely trimmed to a four (4) inch or less, top diameter.
Topwood, cull logs and other material that is four (4) inches or greater in diameter and
that is at least eight (8) feet in length, and that would otherwise not be removed from the
contract area, is to be considered biomass. This material shall be treated as per Special
Provision O. Topwood, cull logs and other material meeting the above dimensions shall
not be bucked into lengths less than eight (8) feet. Tops, limbs and other material not
meeting the minimum dimensions for biomass shall be treated as described below:
Machine treatment of slash (Piling) will be done as follows:
1. Trees may be whole tree skidded to landings, or may be limbed and
topped prior to skidding. If trees are whole tree skidded, the resulting slash will
be placed in piles at the landing. If trees are limbed and topped prior to skidding,
the resulting slash will be pushed into piles using an approved brush piling rake
(“Fleco” or equivalent).
2. Slash piles shall not be more than thirty (30) feet in length, thirty (30)
feet in width, and no more twenty (20) feet in height, unless otherwise authorized
by the Contracting Officer. The minimum distance between piles shall be equal
to, or greater than, the diameter of the piles.
3. Slash piles shall be located so that burning operations will cause only minimal damage to standing live trees. Accordingly, piles will not be constructed
within fifty (50) feet along the exterior edges of the logging units or near groups
of small diameter trees reserved from cutting within the logging units.
4. To facilitate burning, slash piles should be tightly compacted, be mostly
free of dirt, and large stems off the ground should not extend outward more than
ten (10) feet beyond the base of the pile.
5. Burning or other treatment of piled slash shall be done by the
Government.
Lop and scatter treatment of slash will be done as follows:
Limbs, and tops that are four (4) inches in diameter or less at the large end, will
be scattered and all slash will not exceed twenty-four (24) inches in height from
ground level.

Objectives:
The purpose of the proposed action is to open up the overstory canopy and remove trees to reduce
competition with more desirable browse and understory plant species (grasses and forbs).
The need for the proposed action is to:
o Improve soil and vegetative function on upland areas
o Improve overall watershed function within the project area to a condition that meets the
fundamentals or rangeland health as described in 43 CFR 4180.1.
o Maintain existing chainings that were done in and around the 1950's.
o Reduce large fuels in the project area and return the area to a more fire manageable system.
o Provide more forage and habitat for livestock and wildlife in areas that are becoming
fragmented by oil and gas exploration.
The need for the proposed action was identified through consultation with the Tank Mountain Allotment
grazing permittee, BLM natural resource staff, and BLM Fire Management Staff.
Planned_Implementation:
The proposed action is to reduce and remove pinyon pine aA4-juniper trees, by means of a mowing
application with hydro-mower/axe equipment. The following prescription is desired for the project area
as part of the proposed action:
1) Mow all juniper trees with a DBH of 12 inches or less.
2) Mow only Pinyon pine trees with a DBH of 6 inches or less.
3) All browse species such as mountain mahogany; antelope bitterbrush, cliff rose, and oak will be
avoided. Large plants may be cropped to a 2-3ft height
4) Mowing will not be done on any slope greater than 65% (34\xb0).
5) Mosaic "islands&& of trees will be identified, marked and left to provide wildlife cover.
6) Some patches of sagebrush will be mowed, primarily those areas with perennial under story
vegetation.
7) It is preferred that the proposed treatment be done in the fall of 2003 (September-October).
Seeding of perennial grasses and forbs would be done in a few small areas prior to mowing. Seed
would be broadcast prior to mowing so that the litter/mulch provide by the treatment would cover and
protect the seed. Livestock grazing will be deferred from the project area for the following two growing
seasons after completion. Prescribed fire and fuel wood harvest by the public would be used to
maintain the areas after the treatment has taken effect.

Planned_Implementation: The proposed action is to implement the Los Pinos timber sale using the uneven-aged management system through an advertised sale of approximately 1,000 MBF. An entry was made approximately in 1975 by the Los Pinos Pass timber sale. That sale removed approximately 3 MBF/ acre, and not all the volume was removed. No new roads would be constructed, only existing roads would be used and improved. Those roads have serious erosion problems and constructing water dips would lessen the problem. Some of the roads and spurs would possibly be closed, and seeded to grass native to the area. Approximately 220 acres would be partial cut using the selective cutting method. If diseases or bug-killed trees exist, the group selection method would be used. The group selection method of harvesting would create small openings in the presently closed timber canopy. The openings created would average approximately 0.3 acres in size or up to three tree heights (approximately 115 feet X 115 feet). The initial entry would concentrate on removing spruce broom rust infested trees, insect infested trees, trees with low vigor, and dying crowns.

Planned_Implementation:
Proposed Action: The proposed action is for the continued implementation of the Spring
Creek-Dry Creek Vegetation Management Strategy and Environmental Assessment.
Specifically, the proposal is to treat by Lawson Aerator* or similar equipment an area of
approximately 405 acres within four large 1960s-era chainings in the Horsefly area along
Government Springs Road (see maps). The chaining areas are primarily open early mid-seral
pinion-juniper woodland with the stand age < 40 years old. Trees are generally described as
having Christmas tree form with lower limbs touching the ground and tree heights ranging from
6-15 feet and bole diameters at ground height of 3-6 inches. Since the chaining area is the
primary treatment area, no trees greater than about 40 years in age will be impacted by
implementing the proposed action.
*A Lawson Aerator is a tractor with two cylindrical drums equipped with a series of
intermittent blades. The angle of the two drums can be oriented at varying angles to
achieve the desired effect, or percentage of vegetation chopped.
In order to accomplish this, several discrete actions would occur:
1. For the three chainings which lay in Sections 20-21 an area of 206 acres (60% of these
three chainings) would be treated to create early seral vegetation. The equipment would
be adjusted to maximize reduction of existing pinion/juniper and nonnative grasses
(crested wheatgrass). This area would be seeded at that time with a mix of native grasses
and primarily native forbs. The objective for this action, as identified in the Spring
Creek/Dry Creek Strategy, is to reduce non-natives, to create small (<5 acre) patches of
early seral vegetation across 60% of the old chaining, and to avoid treating older stages
of vegetation.
2. 69 acres (20% of these three old chaining) would be treated to create more natural, better
condition early-mid seral vegetation. Objectives are to remove the young trees, reduce
the nonnative grasses and promote and enhance the growth of shrubs and forbs. The
equipment would be set to reduce damage to existing shrubs and herbaceous vegetation
while removing the pinion juniper, and a seed mix consisting primarily of native shrubs
and forbs would be applied.
3. 40 acres (25%) of the chaining in Section 16 would be treated to create early seral
vegetation with the same treatment as proposed in the first action, however the objective
from the strategy is to reduce non-natives, improve conditions, create 3-5 acre patches of
early seral on 25% of the area and avoid more mature patches of existing vegetation.
4. 89 acres (55%) of the chaining in section 16 would be treated to create better condition
early-mid seral vegetation. Objectives are to remove the young trees, reduce the
nonnative grasses and promote and enhance the growth of shrubs and forbs. The
equipment would be set to reduce damage existing shrubs and herbaceous vegetation,
and a different seed mix will be applied, and a seed mix consisting primarily of native
shrubs and forbs would be applied.

The purpose for the proposed action is to change vegetation age classes and vegetation
conditions in specific amounts and patterns on BLM lands in the Lower Horsefly area of the Dry
Creek and Spring Creek watersheds so that they meet, or will be on track to meet vegetation
mosaic objectives. &&Vegetation Mosaic&& is the term used to describe the pattern and amounts of
vegetation age classes across a landscape. There are 10 vegetation mosaic objectives on BLM
lands, each specific to a major vegetation or habitat type, and each designed to promote one of
the following: 1) optimal habitat for at-risk species (Gunnison Sage Grouse), 2) optimal fuels
arrangement to prevent spread of wildfire into areas with residences or power transmission lines,
and 3) natural ecosystem function. Only one objective applies to each part of the landscape&*
where each objective applies is determined by the vegetation type, habitat type or presence of
wildland-urban interface. The Lower Horsefly area has the second objective.
The proposed action will specifically address the reduction of standing fuels to prevent spread of
wildfire into areas with residences and enhancement of natural ecosystem function.

The Fall following the burn and spray treatment, the treated area would be seeded with a
mixture of adapted perennial grasses, forbs and shrubs. Both native and nonnative seed
mixes would be utilized. Native plants would be used to the extent possible in areas
which retain remnant native herbaceous species and have the potential for reestablishment
of native species with available plant material. Based on availability and site suitability,
species may include the following: bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush Squirreltail, great
basin wildrye, Lewis flax, western yarrow, scarlet globemallow, big sagebrush, four-wing
saltbrush or other adapted natives. The perimeter of these treatment blocks may be lined
with strips from 100 to 300 feet (greenstripping) with nonnative species more resistant to
wildfire to break up fuel continuity and protect these areas from future wildfire and
reinvasion by annual weedy species. Nonnative plants will be used in areas that are more
heavily infested with invasive annual species, in areas where suitable adapted natives are

occurrence of wildfire both in wildland urban interface areas and transitional areas
adjacent to more intact shrub habitat. Species mixtures may include plants such as
crested wheatgrass, great basin wildrye, bluegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, forage kochia,
four-wing saltbrush and big sagebrush. Depending upon individual species' seeding
requirements, the seeding/planting would be done using a rangeland drill and/or broadcast
application. Anticipated native and nonnative seed mix areas are identified on map 3. As
more native plant material becomes available either through release of new cultivars or
collection and propagation of locally adapted species, these may be substituted and used
on areas identified for seeding with nonnative mixes.

Objectives:
The objective of the ground seeding treatments is to revegetate the burned area with
a well-adapted array of species that will provide essential forage and cover for greater sagegrouse,
mule deer, and antelope, and will promote structural and species diversity within the
burned area. Objectives will be considered met on the treatment if three seedlings per square
meter are rooted firmly in the ground.
Planned_Implementation: Drill Seeding\r\nDrill seed approximately 2,294 acres of BLM administered lands with a mixture of bluebunch wheatgrass, Snake River wheatgrass, Sandberg\u2019s bluegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, sainfoin, and small burnet. Drill seeding would take place in areas of gentle topography conducive to drill seeding, where recovery of native species was anticipated to be weak or low and areas with the highest threat of annual grass increase. Drill seeding would take place in the fall of 2017 (FY18).
Actual_Implementation: The seed mix was comprised of snake river wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), small\r\nburnet (Sanguisorba minor), sainfoin (Onobrychis viciifolia), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda),\r\nbluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), and squirreltail (Elymus elymoides).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
S2 Drill Seeding
2019 Density Results:
Density: The seed mix was comprised of snake river wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), small
burnet (Sanguisorba minor), sainfoin (Onobrychis viciifolia), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda),
bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), and squirreltail (Elymus elymoides). The
monitoring results show that the rehabilitation objectives of three firmly rooted seedlings per
square meter have been achieved at 18.42 grass seedlings per square meter. Other large form
perennial bunch grasses (Thurber’s needlegrass and Indian ricegrass) are also establishing
themselves at 2.00 grasses per square meter, mainly basin wildrye (Leymus cinereus).


S2 Drill Seeding and S3 Aerial Seeding
2019 AIM Data Results:
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was high (63%) in part due to dominance of cheatgrass
(Bromus tectorum) (34.7% cover) and desert madwort (Alyssum desertorum) (15% cover).
Perennial forbs and shrubs contributed little to cover (11.3% collectively) while Sandberg’s
bluegrass (Poa secunda) contributed significantly to perennial grass cover at 16.3%. Annual
invasive species are still contributing substantially to cover, which will need to be considered
going forward in efforts to control the spread of these species.
2020 AIM Data Results:
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was high (45.7%) in part due to dominance of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) (20.3% cover) and desert madwort (Alyssum desertorum) (2.3% cover). Perennial forbs and shrubs contributed little to cover (7.89% collectively) while Sandberg’s bluegrass (Poa secunda) contributed significantly to perennial grass cover at 16.7%. Annual invasive species are still contributing substantially to cover, which will need to be considered going forward in efforts to control the spread of these species.

Gaps and Erosion:
Pole Creek AIM Plot 01 is located in a Rangeland LOAMY 8-10 P.Z. ecosite (R025XY019NV)
in former / Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis / Achnatherum thurberianum - Achnatherum
hymenoides ( / Wyoming big sagebrush / Thurber's needlegrass - Indian ricegrass) vegetation
communities. Canopy cover had infrequent gaps for the most part, and they varied in size
throughout the plot. Erosion was still high, however, with common pedestals and long, common
water flow patterns. Deposition/runoff was rare. This is a departure from expected site stability
and the establishment of native shrubs and forbs should fill in canopy gaps and decrease erosion.
Pole Creek AIM Plot 02 is located in a Rangeland CLAYPAN 10-12 P.Z. ecosite
(R025XY018NV) in former Artemisia arbuscula / Pseudoroegneria spicata - Achnatherum
thurberianum ( / little sagebrush / bluebunch wheatgrass - Thurber's needlegrass) vegetation
communities. Canopy cover had infrequent gaps for the most part, and they varied in size
throughout the plot. Erosion on this site was also high with widespread pedestals and long, very
common water flow patterns. Deposition/runoff was rare. While some pedestaling is expected,
the high wind and water erosion have destabilized the site and impaired hydrologic function.
2019: Species Richness: An average of twenty-six (26) different plant species were observed within the
two 2,827.4 square meter monitoring plots.
2020: Species Richness: An average of twenty-eight (28) different plant species were observed within the two 2,827.4 square meter monitoring plots.
2019 Recommendations:
The ESR rehabilitation objectives have not been fully met for these treatments. While the drill
seeded grasses are establishing themselves, seeded forbs and shrubs will need more time to
establish and become firmly rooted. There was an allotment closure issued for the Deeth, Devils
Gate, and Pole Creek allotments. The allotment closure objectives of three perennial grasses per
square meter have been met but it is advised that the are remains closed for at least another
growing season until the seeding rehab objectives can be met.
2020 Recommendations:
The ESR rehabilitation objectives have not been fully met for these treatments. While the drill seeded grasses are establishing themselves, seeded forbs and shrubs will need more time to establish and become firmly rooted. There was an allotment closure issued for the Deeth allotment, South and North Steer pastures, where Plots 01 and 02 are located, respectively. The allotment closure objective of three perennial grasses per square meter have not been met it is advised that the area is given more rest so the seeded species may further establish.

ESR 2022 Monitoring Report
S3 Aerial Mix 1/S2 Drill 
Pole Creek AIM Plot 01 is located in a Rangeland LOAMY 8-10 P.Z. ecosite (R025XY019NV) in former Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis / Achnatherum thurberianum - Achnatherum hymenoides (Wyoming big sagebrush / Thurber's needlegrass - Indian ricegrass) vegetation communities. 
Aerial seed mix 1 was comprised of Western yarrow (Achillea millefolium v. occidentalis) and Wyoming Big Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp wyomingensis). 
The seed mix was comprised of snake river wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), small burnet (Sanguisorba minor), sainfoin (Onobrychis viciifolia), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), and squirreltail (Elymus elymoides).
Density Results 
2020: The rehab objectives of 1 non-native shrub and 1 seeded forb per square meter have not been met, yet. The rehab objective of 0.3 native shrubs per square meter have also not been met. No shrubs were observed within the density frames of either plot and 0.17 forb seedlings per square meter were observed in Plot 01. (Drill) The monitoring results show that the rehabilitation objectives of three firmly rooted seedlings per square meter have not been achieved at 0.00 grass seedlings per square meter. Other large form perennial bunch grasses (Thurber’s needlegrass and squirreltail) are establishing themselves at 1.91 grasses per square meter, mainly Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda). 
2022: The rehabilitation objectives of 1 non-native shrub and 1 seeded forb per square meter have not been met. The rehab objective of 0.3 native shrubs per square meter have also not been met. No seeded shrubs or seeded forbs were observed in the density squares but 10.08 seeded grasses/m2 were observed. However, native regrowth of grasses and forbs was strong and shrubs were present as well. 
AIM Data Results 
Cover 
2020: Average foliar canopy cover was high (45.7%) in part due to dominance of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) (20.3% cover) and desert madwort (Alyssum desertorum) (2.3% cover). Perennial forbs and shrubs contributed little to cover (7.89% collectively) while Sandberg’s bluegrass (Poa secunda) contributed significantly to perennial grass cover at 16.7%. Annual invasive species are still contributing substantially to cover, which will need to be considered going forward in efforts to control the spread of these species.
2022: Average foliar cover was moderately low at 38.0%, a decrease of 17.3% since 2020. The most dominant indicator present was annual grass at 9.6% with perennial grasses and forbs following with near equal representation at 6.7% and 6.3% respectively. Shrubs were the lowest they’ve been observed at only 0.4% total.
Gaps and Erosion 
2020: Canopy cover had infrequent gaps for the most part, and they varied in size throughout the plot. Erosion was still high, however, with common pedestals and long, common water flow patterns. Deposition/runoff was rare. This is a departure from expected site stability and the establishment of native shrubs and forbs should fill in canopy gaps and decrease erosion. 
2022: Canopy gaps increased significantly in each size range since 2020. The most frequent gap size was >200cm at 32.9%, by far the highest it has been observed since monitoring began in 2019. Additionally, gaps sized 101-200cm was observed at 20.9%, almost equal to the amount of gaps 25-50cm and 51-100cm combined. However, only common waterflow patterns were observed, an improvement in soil stability since 2020, so more likely the increase in gap cover is related to the drop in total foliar cover than site and soil erosion.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness was moderately high at 30 individual species identified. The number of perennial forbs accounts for more than half of the total species identified and therefore perennial species greatly outnumbered the annual species on the plot.

While the drill seeded grasses are establishing themselves, seeded forbs and shrubs will need more time to establish and become firmly rooted. There was an allotment closure issued for the Deeth allotment. The allotment closure objective of three perennial grasses per square meter have not been met it is advised that the area is given more rest so the seeded species may further establish.

Density Results 
2020: The rehab objectives of 1 non-native shrub and 1 seeded forb per square meter have not been met, yet. The rehab objective of 0.3 native shrubs per square meter have also not been met. No shrubs were observed within the density frames of either plot and 0.17 forb seedlings per square meter were observed in Plot 01. Other large form perennial bunch grasses (Thurber’s needlegrass and squirreltail) are establishing themselves at 1.91 grasses per square meter, mainly Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda). 
2022: The rehabilitation objectives of 1 non-native shrub and 1 seeded forb per square meter have not been met. The rehab objective of 0.3 native shrubs per square meter have also not been met. No seeded shrubs or seeded forbs were observed in the density squares but 10.08 seeded grasses/m2 were observed. However, native regrowth of grasses and forbs was strong and shrubs were present as well. 
AIM Data Results 
Cover 
2020: Average foliar canopy cover was high (45.7%) in part due to dominance of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) (20.3% cover) and desert madwort (Alyssum desertorum) (2.3% cover). Perennial forbs and shrubs contributed little to cover (7.89% collectively) while Sandberg’s bluegrass (Poa secunda) contributed significantly to perennial grass cover at 16.7%. Annual invasive species are still contributing substantially to cover, which will need to be considered going forward in efforts to control the spread of these species.
2022: Average foliar cover was moderately low at 38.0%, a decrease of 17.3% since 2020. The most dominant indicator present was annual grass at 9.6% with perennial grasses and forbs following with near equal representation at 6.7% and 6.3% respectively. Shrubs were the lowest they’ve been observed at only 0.4% total.
Gaps and Erosion 
2020: Canopy cover had infrequent gaps for the most part, and they varied in size throughout the plot. Erosion was still high, however, with common pedestals and long, common water flow patterns. Deposition/runoff was rare. This is a departure from expected site stability and the establishment of native shrubs and forbs should fill in canopy gaps and decrease erosion. 
2022: Canopy gaps increased significantly in each size range since 2020. The most frequent gap size was >200cm at 32.9%, by far the highest it has been observed since monitoring began in 2019. Additionally, gaps sized 101-200cm was observed at 20.9%, almost equal to the amount of gaps 25-50cm and 51-100cm combined. However, only common waterflow patterns were observed, an improvement in soil stability since 2020, so more likely the increase in gap cover is related to the drop in total foliar cover than site and soil erosion.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness was moderately high at 30 individual species identified. The number of perennial forbs accounts for more than half of the total species identified and therefore perennial species greatly outnumbered the annual species on the plot.

Objectives: The primary objective of the treatment is to seed areas of the burn that are at high risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion. Due to these risks coupled with moderate annual precipitation (8-10 inches), a seed mix consisting of native species (Indian Ricegrass, Big bluegrass, Snake River wheatgrass, Blue flax and Scarlet globemallow, ) was selected to decrease soil erosion and the possibility of invasion by non-native species.\r\nAreas identified for treatment are those with the highest vegetation mortality or most at risk for cheatgrass invasion or major erosion. Drill seed approximately 4,350 acres with a mixture of Indian ricegrass, Sherman bluegrass, Snake River wheatgrass, Great Basin wildrye and blue flax. This seeding will be completed using a rangeland or minimum till drill.


Drill seeding is being proposed to address soil and water stabilization issues on the Hepworth Fire, as well as deterring invasive species.  A native mix of Indian ricegrass, Sherman bluegrass, Snake River wheatgrass, Great Basin wildrye and blue flax will be seeded on 4,350 acres of mid elevation sites that burned hot, with high vegetation loss that are appropriate for drill seeding. 
The cost of ground seeding is $382,065. Post-fire assessments identified only areas for treatment that are at highest risk for permanent site conversion. The size of the area and cost of rehabilitating these sites will be much smaller following the current proposal.  Should these proposals not be implemented and cheatgrass invasion and major erosion occur, the cost and size of the restoration project could be enormous.

Planned_Implementation:
Total juniper reduction (cutting and piling) - The treatment consists of cutting all expansion juniper within portions of a project unit. Juniper will be cut and piled prior to follow-up treatments; this could be accomplished by nonmotorized or motorized means. 
Commercial use of cut expansion juniper - Downed expansion juniper could be collected for firewood, ornamental use, or other uses. Section 113(b) (2) of the Steens Act allows for the removal of legally downed juniper in the CMPA outside of wilderness and WSAs. 
Selective juniper reduction (cutting and piling) - Treatments could vary from cutting every third tree in juniper pockets to limbing and girdling expansion juniper found in dense stands. Juniper could be cut and piled prior to follow-up treatments; this could be accomplished by nonmotorized or motorized means. 
Every third tree cutting involves felling trees into juniper pockets to provide ladder fuels for remaining junipers. This method has worked well in areas with moderately dense juniper, steep slopes, and remnant ground fuels to carry fire between juniper pockets. In areas of moderate slopes this technique may be limited as fire needs more ladder fuels and a mechanism such as high or up-slope winds to carry fire through surrounding tree canopies. 
Droop cutting involves cutting lower limbs of expansion juniper so they droop to the ground. Limbs are not severed from the tree bole; instead they are cut three-fourths through from the top down. This method results in ladder fuels still attached to the base of standing trees. As fire carries through juniper stands, dead limbs ignite and carry fire into the tree canopy. This technique is limited by topography and fuel conditions required to carry fire between juniper pockets. Advantages to this technique include a minimized cutting time to treat stands of juniper, and the majority of fuels is left in a vertical arrangement above ground surface thereby reducing heat effects to soils and other resources (primarily cultural). A further advantage is the post-treatment Project Area resembles the result of a wildfire. 
The limb and girdle method involves scoring and cutting limbs around the base of the juniper as well as cutting through the cambium layer. This technique results in dead material at the base of juniper trees providing a receptive fuel bed for fire, while increasing chances of killing the trees. The limb and girdle method works well in dense stands of juniper with little to no understory to carry fire. As with droop cutting, the limb and girdle method results in juniper remaining upright which keeps the majority of the fuels away from fragile soils and mimics the lower intensity of a wildfire event.

Objectives for the White Mule Fire Rehabilitation Plan are as follows:
1. Stabilize soils and reduce future fire hazards in cheatgrass dominated
areas by reducing the re-establishment of annual grasses and weeds, through
seeding adapted non-native species. Protect the rehabilitation effort by
excluding livestock grazing in the Dry Creek Pasture for at least two
growing seasons (i .e., first full year and until seed ripe the second year).
2. Reduce soil erosion, restore perennial cover, restore vegetative structure
for wildlife, increase effective precipitation by capturing and holding snow
during the winter months by establishing a deep rooted shrub component in
the plant community.
3. Preclude cheatgrass invasion by augmenting the native plant community
(Wyoming big sagebrush, bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail) via
seeding native perennial species.
4. Protect the seedings and burned area by reducing the Wild Horse
population numbers from 219 to between 50 and 75 animals to insure the
health and vigor of the remaining horses in the HMA.
5. Reduce future burned acreage by establishing a 200 foot green strip along
the northern perimeter and the two-track road bisecting the burned area.
The green strip would buffer weed invasion and most importantly, buffer
future wildland fire spread.
6. Restore the boundary fence for protection of the seedings and burned
area.
7. Repair the road damage for public access and decreased soil erosion.

Objectives: The purpose and need for rehabilitation includes the following: to minimize soil loss,  preserve on-site productivity, reduce the re-invasion of undesirable flammable annual plants reduce size and extent of highly flammable fuel types, reduce the threat of destruction of private property due to wildfire, reduce the potential for widespread noxious weed invasion\r\nThis need can be met by establishing desirable perennial plant cover
Planned_Implementation:
Two basic seed mixes would be used in the rangeland drills, a greenstrip or nonnative mix
and a native plant mix. Approximately 12,000 acres would be seeded to the native mix and
10,000 acres to the nonnative mix. The mixes may be altered slightly depending upon seed
availability and/or soil types. For instance compatible forbs or shrubs such as globemallow
(Sphaercea spp.), lupine (Lupinus spp.) or four wing saltbrush (Atriplex canescens) if available
may be substituted in suitable soil and habitat types. Forage kochia (Kochia prostrata) would
be substituted for four wing saltbrush only on the proposed greens trip running from near Alkali
Spring to South Jacobson Gulch. In extremely sandy soils other species such as Indian
Ricegrass (Oryzopsis hyrnenoides), if available, may be substituted for other native grass
species. In soils with higher clay content species such as western wheatgrass (Pascopyrum
smithii) may be included. The seed when mixed will be treated with a organic seed coating to
enhance germination and seedling survival.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Vale District Bureau of Land Management (BLM) proposes to implement a multi-year, phased fuels management and ecological restoration project within the Mormon Basin / Pedro Mountain Planning Area in the Baker Resource Area. Silvicultural thinning, conifer (conifer, Ponderosa Pine, Douglas-fir) cutting, herbicide application, and prescribed fire activities would be primary management tools.
Fire-dependent ecological communities in the project area lack resiliency to wildfire, insects, disease, and other disturbances. Coniferous forests, shrublands, and riparian areas that function as those under historical conditions are more stable, support greater wildlife species diversity; and enhance watershed function. Ecosystems that are deficient of these conditions are likely to be especially vulnerable to the increased fire frequencies and intensities that will come with a changing climate.
High fuel loading within coniferous forests and woodlands has increased the risks of ground fires becoming crown fires, and small fires becoming stand-replacement wildfires. Reducing hazardous fuels within forested stands will help protect life, property, and resource values, as well as increase the safety of personnel involved in wildland fire management actions.
The quality and productivity of browse and forage species available to wildlife in the project area needs to be improved. Bunchgrasses and forbs are important forage for elk, mule deer, bighorn sheep, and avian species, and have been reduced or are completely absent in plant communities undergoing conversion to juniper woodlands and in closed canopy mixed conifer forest stands. Key wildlife browse species such as aspen, bitterbrush and mountain mahogany are declining under the influence of conifer encroachment.
This environmental assessment (EA) examines the potential effects of: continuing existing management (the No Action Alternative); implementation of a Proposed Action (Alternative 2); as well as an additional action alternative (Alternative 3) within the project area. An interdisciplinary team of specialists from the Vale District conducted the environmental analysis. The EA will supply the decision-maker, the Baker Resource Area Field Office Manager, with information to utilize in the decision-making process in compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). The EA will allow BLM to determine if there are significant impacts not already analyzed in the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for the Vale District’s Baker Resource Management Plan (BRMP FEIS, USDI-BLM, 1989). If the decision-maker determines that there are significant impacts associated with the project, then analysis of effects will be transitioned to an EIS analysis and planning document. If the EA shows that there are no significant impacts associated with the project, then preparation of a Finding of No Significant Impact is appropriate. A decision record may be signed by the Baker Field Office Manager following public comment on the EA to document the decision.
The purpose of the Proposed Action is to achieve management objectives described in the Baker Resource Area Resource Management Plan (RMP) Record of Decision within the Mormon Basin / Pedro Mountain planning area by:
Reducing hazardous fuels
Restoring plant communities
Improving wildlife habitat diversity
The need for action is based on degraded landscape conditions and threats to resources, private property and fire fighter safety. This was determined by comparing existing conditions of hazardous fuels, wildfire risks, rangeland plant communities, forest health, and wildlife habitat to the desired condition for those resources.
Chapter 2 provides the analytical basis for comparison of the action alternatives to the No Action Alternative. Chapter 3 (Affected Environment) summarizes the existing physical, biological, social, and economic environments of the project area.

Objectives: Reduce Hazardous Fuels 0-10" by 95%.\r\nThin over stock stands and Ladder fuels.\r\nPromote Healthy Forest.
Planned_Implementation:
MECHANICAL THINNING AND CUTTING
Variable density thinning would be the primary activity applied under the silvicultural thinning treatments in the Proposed Action. Variable density thinning involves a combination of commercial and non-commercial thinning techniques that results in retention of trees grouped in small dispersed patches with ladder fuels and crown fuels that are substantially reduced. Varied tree spacing, as opposed to even spacing is desirable. Tree clumping for stand diversity will be left as well as creating small openings to create a “gappy” appearance.
NON-COMMERCIAL THINNING
Non-commercial thinning involves manually cutting non-merchantable trees (< 9” diameter) to reduce fuel laddering and/or help achieve specific resource objectives. Non-commercial thinning would be accomplished with chainsaws or hand tools. The activity fuels generated by this activity would be piled or possibly burned as jackpots. Most slash generated between December 1 and July 1 would be removed from treatment units to guard against tree mortality from Ips bark beetle attacks (See Section 2.5, Project Design Elements). In aspen stands up to 1/3 of older, dying aspen maybe cut and left on site to rejuvenate sprouting.
COMMERCIAL THINNING
Commercial thinning removes merchantable (> 9” diameter) trees to reduce the fuels in a forested canopy that allow for the development of high intensity crown fires. It also improves the health and growth rate of trees remaining in a stand following treatment by removing stressed/diseased trees and reducing competition stress of remaining trees.
Commercial harvest activities conducted on slopes of less than 35% would be performed using ground-based equipment such as a mechanical harvesters, tractors, and rubber-tired skidders. Harvest activities occurring on terrain with slopes exceeding 35% would be conducted with a skyline logging system or by helicopter. Slash generated by the commercial harvest would be removed to a landing for disposal by burning or for biomass utilization if economically feasible. Otherwise, activity fuels generated by commercial harvest would be piled within treatments units for burning. Commercial thinning within the project area would be conducted under timber sales or possibly under stewardship contracts.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Vale District Bureau of Land Management (BLM) proposes to implement a multi-year, phased fuels management and ecological restoration project within the Mormon Basin / Pedro Mountain Planning Area in the Baker Resource Area. Silvicultural thinning, conifer (conifer, Ponderosa Pine, Douglas-fir) cutting, herbicide application, and prescribed fire activities would be primary management tools.
Fire-dependent ecological communities in the project area lack resiliency to wildfire, insects, disease, and other disturbances. Coniferous forests, shrublands, and riparian areas that function as those under historical conditions are more stable, support greater wildlife species diversity; and enhance watershed function. Ecosystems that are deficient of these conditions are likely to be especially vulnerable to the increased fire frequencies and intensities that will come with a changing climate.
High fuel loading within coniferous forests and woodlands has increased the risks of ground fires becoming crown fires, and small fires becoming stand-replacement wildfires. Reducing hazardous fuels within forested stands will help protect life, property, and resource values, as well as increase the safety of personnel involved in wildland fire management actions.
The quality and productivity of browse and forage species available to wildlife in the project area needs to be improved. Bunchgrasses and forbs are important forage for elk, mule deer, bighorn sheep, and avian species, and have been reduced or are completely absent in plant communities undergoing conversion to juniper woodlands and in closed canopy mixed conifer forest stands. Key wildlife browse species such as aspen, bitterbrush and mountain mahogany are declining under the influence of conifer encroachment.
This environmental assessment (EA) examines the potential effects of: continuing existing management (the No Action Alternative); implementation of a Proposed Action (Alternative 2); as well as an additional action alternative (Alternative 3) within the project area. An interdisciplinary team of specialists from the Vale District conducted the environmental analysis. The EA will supply the decision-maker, the Baker Resource Area Field Office Manager, with information to utilize in the decision-making process in compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). The EA will allow BLM to determine if there are significant impacts not already analyzed in the Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for the Vale District’s Baker Resource Management Plan (BRMP FEIS, USDI-BLM, 1989). If the decision-maker determines that there are significant impacts associated with the project, then analysis of effects will be transitioned to an EIS analysis and planning document. If the EA shows that there are no significant impacts associated with the project, then preparation of a Finding of No Significant Impact is appropriate. A decision record may be signed by the Baker Field Office Manager following public comment on the EA to document the decision.
The purpose of the Proposed Action is to achieve management objectives described in the Baker Resource Area Resource Management Plan (RMP) Record of Decision within the Mormon Basin / Pedro Mountain planning area by:
Reducing hazardous fuels
Restoring plant communities
Improving wildlife habitat diversity
The need for action is based on degraded landscape conditions and threats to resources, private property and fire fighter safety. This was determined by comparing existing conditions of hazardous fuels, wildfire risks, rangeland plant communities, forest health, and wildlife habitat to the desired condition for those resources.
Chapter 2 provides the analytical basis for comparison of the action alternatives to the No Action Alternative. Chapter 3 (Affected Environment) summarizes the existing physical, biological, social, and economic environments of the project area.

Objectives: The purpose of the treatment is to help quickly re-establish native vegetation to provide habitat value and prevent the spread of invasive species and to stabilize soils and reduce sediment run-off.  This treatment is expected to be moderately to highly effective based on similar treatments in other areas.
Planned_Implementation: This treatment will use local seed stock of native species to the greatest extent possible.  Seed will be applied in high burn intensity areas in the late fall of 2010 using a helicopter with a seeder attachment.
Actual_Implementation: Aerial seeding followed by harrowing in Nov 2012.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Success of the aerial seeding appears to be
variable, in part due to an unexpected seedbank of prickly lettuce that sprouted fairly densely in
some areas. Prickly lettuce appeared to have increased in much of the burned area, including
outside of the harrowed area, and it is suspected that it developed a good seed bank following
2011 and 2012 growing seasons and the seed is easily carried by the wind, resulting in obvious
expansion in 2013. Areas were it sprouted the densest were treated using a wick to prevent
damage to establishing seedlings. Prickly lettuce is expected to decline naturally as time goes on
following the fire and as seedling become established.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Issues relate to resource problems caused by the wildfire and include both the immediate wildfire effects as well as effects predicted to occur as a result of the wildfire.  Determining the appropriate funding code must be based on the scope of the issue, purpose of the treatment, and the availability of funds.  
EMERGENCY STABILIZATION ISSUES

Emergency Stabilization Objectives:  “determine the need for and to prescribe and implement emergency treatments to minimize threats to life or property or to stabilize and prevent unacceptable degradation to natural and cultural resources resulting from the effects of a fire.”  620DM3.4

Emergency Stabilization Priorities:  1) Human Life and Safety, and 2) Property and unique biological (designated Critical Habitat for Federal and State listed, proposed or candidate threatened and endangered species) and significant heritage sites.  620DM3.7

Issue 1 - Human Life and Safety.  Replacing or repairing minor facilities essential to public health and safety when no other protection options are available.  

Parts of the burned area contain abandoned irrigation structures associated with the irrigation canal that runs along much of the burn perimeter.  Fencing that prevented access to many of the structures was burned in the fire.  The deteriorated condition of these structures presents a hazard to life and safety (i.e., large holes in concrete or exposed, jagged metal). Fences need to be repaired to prevent access to these structures.  In addition, drainage culverts that were partially blocked before the fire may not have the capacity for increased flows that are likely to occur after the fire.

Issue 2 - Soil/Water Stabilization.  Placing structures to slow soil and water movement, stabilizing soil to prevent loss or degradation or productivity, increasing road drainage frequency and/or capacity to handle additional post-fire runoff, installing protective fences or barriers to protect treated or recovering areas.  

The burned area contains steep slopes and drainage bottoms that are highly susceptible to erosion. The fire has resulted in hydrophobic soil conditions in areas where burn intensity was moderate to severe.  The burned area is located upslope of designated critical habitat for Columbia River steelhead and both agricultural and residential areas and associated infrastructure such as roads, powerlines, and irrigation systems.  Heavy rains or spring run-off could result in soil movement and/or flash-flood conditions.

Issue 3 - Habitat for Federal/State Listed, Proposed, or Candidate Species.  Seeding or planting to prevent permanent impairment of designated Critical Habitat for Federal and State listed, proposed or candidate threatened and endangered species.  

The burned area is within the WDFW’s Rattlesnake Hills Greater Sage-Grouse Management Unit.  The greater sage-grouse is a federal Candidate species and is listed as Threatened by the State of Washington.  The Washington population of greater sage-grouse is listed as the Columbia Basin Distinct Population Segment by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.  The fire removed sage-brush habitat that is considered to be essential to the recovery of the Washington population of greater sage-grouse.

The burned area also supports a population of Tauschia hooveri, a plant listed as a Federal Species of Concern and Threatened by the State of Washington.  The species is susceptible to disturbance and subsequent competition from invasive species, both of which have been exacerbated by the fire.

Issue 4 - Critical Heritage Resources.  Stabilizing critical heritage resources, patrolling, camouflaging, burying significant heritage sites to prevent looting.  

The burned area has documented cultural sites and is known to be a cultural “hot spot”.  The area is also a popular recreation area and exposed cultural sites may be susceptible to looting and vandalism.  

Issue 5 - Invasive Plants and Weeds.  Seeding to prevent establishment of invasive plants, and direct treatment of invasive plants.  Such actions will be specified in the emergency stabilization plan only when immediate action is required and when standard treatments are used that have been validated by monitoring data from previous projects, or when there is documented research establishing the effectiveness of such actions.  Using integrated pest management techniques to minimize the establishment of non-native invasive species within the burned area.  When there is an existing approved management plan that addresses non-native invasive species, emergency stabilization treatments may be used to stabilize the invasive species.  

Arid-land shrub-steppe ecosystems throughout this geographic region have been shown to be susceptible to fire induced conversion to annual grasslands that results from shortened fire-returned intervals and invasive species.  There were several species of weeds and other invasive plants already established in the area prior to the fire, including various knapweed species and scotch thistle.  Invasive species are especially prevalent along the old irrigation canal and roadways on private property bordering BLM lands.  BLM’s small parcel size results in increased edge effect and greater susceptibility to invasive species.  Research from nearby Arid Lands Ecological Reserve on post-fire treatments has shown increased resiliency to invasive species in areas that were treated with aerial seeding and herbicide applications.
