Objectives: The objective of the treatment is to establish 40 sagebrush plants per acre at the 3rd year after\r\nplanting. 3rd year post-planting success will be based on: Fully successful=40 or more plants/acre; Partially\r\nsuccessful=1-39 surviving plants/acre; Unsuccessful=Less than 1 surviving plant/acre.
Planned_Implementation: Seedling planting contract has been awarded and grow out is ongoing\r\nwith planting planned for Fall 2016 and Fall of 2017.
Actual_Implementation:
Seedling planting completed Nov 2016. Additional grass and forb
seedlings (33,000) were planted instead of drill seeding on
approximately 1,200 acres. These areas had generally good
recovery but had some gaps, so seedling were planted in the gap
areas rather than drilling the entire area.

Approximately 33,000 seedlings were planted, half in the southern area and half in the northern area.


Douglas (South) Fire
Task 2 seeding was originally planned for 553 acres. 22 acres were drill seeded in an
area that also received glyphosate treatments for P. bulbosa. The remaining 531 acres were
modified for plug installation instead of the original seeding treatment and planted during the
Fall of 2016.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Douglas (North) Fire area
Comparisons between the drill-seeding and seedling planting treatments show that the seedling treatment area had lower bare soil cover and higher cover of biological soil crusts, annual graminoids, perennial graminoids, and invasive graminoids. The drill-seeding treatment had higher cover of bare soil, annual forbs, perennial forbs, GRSG preferred forbs, non-graminoid invasive, sagebrush, and other shrubs (Table 38). LPI results show that the seedling planting treatment had higher foliar coverage of seeded species Festuca idahoensis (FEID) and Poa secunda (POSE) than the drill seeding treatment, while the drill seeding treatment had only slightly higher foliar cover (2.9%) of Pseudoroegneria spicata (PSSP6) than the seedling planting treatment had (Table 39). There were a few species that were detected in previous years that were not detected during the 2018 field season. This could possibly be attributed to the time of year of surveying and species identification by observers.

Douglas (South)
Only two AIM monitoring plots fell within the boundaries of the treatment area for treatments that were completed during time of survey. One plot, LPI_0778_514 (R008XY102WA) fell within the herbicide treatment area that was scheduled for seeding later in the season. The second plot LPI_0778_51 (R008X103WA) fell within the seeded treatment that received no herbicide. An additional plot LPI_0778 40 (R008XY102WA) landed within the modified plug treatment area that was scheduled for planting later on in the season. Two of the three AIM monitoring plots will eventually be located in the seeding/plug installation treatment areas, however, these treatments were scheduled to occur after the plots had been sampled for the 2016 season

2017 and 2018 Soil Stability results for the different treatment area are shown in Table 23. The Ecological Site Description reference sheets list that soil stability class values are estimated to be 5-6 at the surface under perennial plant cover (covered) and 4-5 at the surface in the interspaces (no cover). There was an increase in soil stability from 2017 to 2018 for both treatment areas.

The 2017 and 2018 Species Richness results for the different treatment areas are shown in Table 24. There was an overall increase in species count across both treatments, with drill seeding without spray having a slightly higher total species count.

Planned_Implementation:
Douglas (South):
Before the Douglas Complex fire, drill seeding had occurred on 66 acres of BLM land in
Douglas south in March 2015. Seeding was stopped early because of the excessive coverage of
Poa bulbosa in the area. After the fire event, there was a major increase in cover of P. bulbosa
and the stage of its growth threatened the success of the native plants seeding. Following this
discovery, approximately 179 acres dominated by P. bulbosa were treated with glyphosate. The
remaining 158 acres was scheduled for seeding during the Fall of 2016 after GBI crews
conducted AIM monitoring.

Douglas (North): 
Proposed treatments within the burn area included ground seeding of perennial bunchgrasses,
sagebrush seedling planting, weeds monitoring, and herbicide treatment (Ellis 2016d). The
seeding treatment was originally proposed for 880 acres to be drill seeded, however, only 240
acres were drill seeded during the fall of 2016, after AIM monitoring was completed. The
remaining 640 acres will be modified to installing native plugs, with planting scheduled to occur
in 2017.


Ground-based seeding would use minimum-till drills. Native, locally sourced species would be seeded with application targeted for November 2016
Actual_Implementation:
General notes and items of importance during implementation.
Based on the current vegetation conditions, it was decided that the
best approach was to drill seed approximately 420 acres (180 in
southern area and 240 acres in northern area), and convert the
remaining treatment acres to plug installation. Approximately
33,000 seedlings were planted, half in the southern area and half in
the northern area.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2020: The drill-seeding treatment had higher cover of bare soil, annual forbs, perennial forbs, GRSG preferred forbs, non-graminoid invasive, sagebrush, and other shrubs (Table 38). LPI results show that the seedling planting treatment had higher foliar coverage of seeded species Festuca idahoensis (FEID) and Poa secunda (POSE) than the drill seeding treatment, while the drill seeding treatment had only slightly higher foliar cover (2.9%) of Pseudoroegneria spicata (PSSP6) than the seedling planting treatment had (Table 39). There were a few species that were detected in previous years that were not detected during the 2018 field season. This could possibly be attributed to the time of year of surveying and species identification by observers.

2018: FY2018: Monitoring of seeding treatments implemented in spring and fall of 2016 indicate low
establishment of bluebunch wheatgrass in the areas seeded in fall of 2016 compared to areas
seeded in spring of 2016. This is most likely due to high competition of crested wheatgrass reestablishing
in these areas. Analysis of this data is ongoing and will be used to inform future
decision.

- - - - - EA - - - - -

The proposed action is to selectively harvest Douglas fir trees from an area...

The purpose of the proposed action is to: (1) reduce the amount of dwarf mistletoe in the stand by selectively harvesting those trees that are currently dead and dying, or at least moderately infested with the parasite. In addition, some non-infected but overmature trees will be removed. (2) Salvage any trees that have been infected by the Douglas fir bark beetle. (3) Thin that part of the stand (Unit III) that consists of trees predominately in the 6 - 10" DBR class so that the residual stems will have sufficient growing space to continue the most rapid growth as possible. Only those trees showing the most desirable characteristics will be left for further growth.

- - - - - Contract - - - - -

Timber reserved from cutting: All timber except trees marked at breast height and at the base with orange, yellow or blue paint.

1. Prior to the , commencement of operations, the Purchaser shall obtain from the Authorized ' Officer written approval of a written operations and logging plan commensurate with the terms and conditions of the contract which shall include measures needed to assure protection of the environment and watershed. All logging shall be done in accordance with the plan. Tractor or wheeled type equipment will not be permitted to operate in or through drainage courses.

2. Before beginning operations on the contract area for the first time, or after a shutdown of ten (10) or more days, the Purchaser shall notify the Authorized Officer in writing of the date he plans to begin operations. He shall notify the Authorized Officer in writing if he intends to cease operations for any period of ten (10) days or more.

3. All trees shall be cut so that the resultant stump height on the uphill side shall not exceed twelve (12) inches.

4. All snags, culls and marginal trees designated for cutting shall be felled concurrently with all other trees designated for cutting in the harvest area shown on Exhibit A-I.

5. All yarding shall be done with crawler type equipment, rubber tired skidder, or with horses.

6. No cutting, yarding or loading is permitted outside the harvest area shown in Exhibit A-I.

7. All landings shall be placed at the approximate locations shown on Exhibit A-I unless otherwise authorized by the Authorized Officer prior to any logging activity.

8. All reproduction, where possible, shall be protected.

9. Dozer blades will be removed for yarding unless the operator can demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Authorized Officer that he can operate such equipment without damage to the reserved trees.

10. Tractor trails shall not exceed grades of 35% and shall be limited to designated locations authorized in advance by the Authorized Officer.

11. Only those trees marked may be cut and removed.

12. Cutting of any and all timber is restricted to between the dates June 1 and October 31. These dates may be adjusted by the Authorized Officer due to weather conditions of each season.

Objectives: ...aerial seeding approximately 7,387 acres of burned vegetation with Basin big sagebrush.
Planned_Implementation: Implementation of aerial seeding would be monitored through contract administration. The Contract Officer and his/her representative (COTR) would ensure seed is purchased and meets BLM Standards. Inspections would be documented by the COTR in an inspection diary.
Actual_Implementation:
Seed was purchased for BAR revegetation treatments on 8/28.

The seed lot that was purchased on 8/28 was sent to a certified seed laboratory for testing to meet BLM Standards (i.e., no Idaho noxious weeds and minimum 0.765 PLS).

- - - - - 2007 MonFund - - - - -

The aerial seeding was monitored during the 2007.

- - - - - 2008 MonFund - - - - -

The aerial seeding was monitored during the 2007 and 2008 field seasons.

Monitoring in 2008 consisted of 2 transects in chained and seeded areas, and 3 transects in drill-seeded areas and 3 transects in reference areas that were burned but not seeded (see Fig. 1). Each transect was 20 x 300 ft., thereby covering a total area of 6,000 ft. Big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) plants were counted within transects. Yarrow, flax and penstemon were not monitored in 2008.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring conducted in the chained area showed that this area had the highest diversity of perennial grass species.  This area had very little crested wheatgrass present, however there was little present prior to the fire.  Monitoring showed that the aerial seeding objective was achieved at the excellent level. 

The transects that were conducted in the acres of the seeding, found the existing burned vegetation recovering, but found very little of the seeded species. However, it may be just too soon to tell how well this seeding will take. More monitoring will be done in 2008 and provide a better overall picture on results.

There were sage brush, white yarrow, Lewis flax, and Wasatch penstemon seedlings found through out the burn, although it is almost impossible to tell if they are natural or from the aerial seeding. This area will be monitored next year to assess the effectiveness of the aerial seeding.

Sagebrush seeding monitoring was done by reading sagebrush density belt transects at each of the eight previously established transect sites. A three hundred foot baseline tape was stretched at the site, and three transects were read at random points along the baseline. Each belt transect was three hundred feet long and 16 feet wide. One sagebrush plant was found in the burned, drill-seeded site in 2008. No other sagebrush plants were counted in reference, drill- or aerial-seeded sites (Table 1). The dominant and almost exclusive vegetation is crested wheatgrass. Clearly these aerial and drill-seeding methods are not effective and should be reviewed before further implementation at other sites.

Lessons learned:
The practice of chaining dead juniper trees was particularly devastating on soil structure and revegetation. Fig. 2 (below) shows an unchained area allowed to naturally recover. While damage from the burn is still apparent, reasonable revegetation compared with surrounding reference sites occurred. Chained areas (Figs. 3-6), although seeded with native vegetation, show lower levels of both native and exotic revegetation and often present large patches of bare ground (Figs. 3 and 4). In areas with gentle slopes, water runoff combined with disturbances from cattle have caused large gullies through the loose soil (Figs. 5 and 6).

Objectives: The BLM SLFO would reduce the potential of extreme fire danger by reducing big sagebrush and diversifying the existing plant community while improving wildlife habitat.
Planned_Implementation:
The treatment would occur in each of the three polygons (see map, Appendix A) within
the Big Creek, Stuart, and Woodruff Pastures equaling 20 - 40% of the total 2,313 acre
analysis area which would equal approximately 530 acres.
The mechanical treatments would be implemented in 2003. Maintenance activities may
be necessary 2 - 25 years after the project is completed, such as seeding or crunching to
meet the objectives stated in the need for the proposed action. A fence would be installed
prior to the 2004 grazing season.
A tractor/dozer would pull a brush cruncher (pasture aerator) which would crush, tear,
and chop older stagnate age classes of sagebrush allowing younger, supple age classes to
spring back with little or no harm; therefore, reducing the risk of large wildland fire
growth by breaking up the continuity of the current fuel arrangement. The brush
cruncher is a useful tool, which leaves minimal ground disturbance, leaving the surface
cover intact while creating divots for good soil to seed contact.
Treated areas would be seeded by attaching a drop seeder to the back of the aerator with a
grass/forb/browse seed mixture (see Seed Species List, Appendix D), which could
support wildlife species year-round in the area.
During the treatment, the aerator would create a mosaic pattern by following the natural
contours of the landscape during the fall season or as weather permits. The mosaic
patterns would range in size generally less than 200 yards wide with a maximum of 40%
of the area treated. A support vehicle for the contractor would need to access the site
each day and one BLM truck would access the site each day for inspection. The road
system around the site is adequate to meet these needs without driving off-road.
Actual_Implementation: The pasture aerator treatment at the Big Three was implemented in October and November of 2003 and April and May of2004. A contractor with a tractor and pasture aerator crunched and seeded 531 acres of sagebrush-steppe in a mosaic pattern within the Big Three project areas during this period.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: We achieved all of the objectives of the Big Three project.

build a temporary fence and take whatever measures are necessary to keep

the third growing season , if by examination it is determined that the
plants are properly rooted and capable of withstanding livestock grazing.

grazing of livestock will be delayed until the plants are capable of
withstanding grazing by livestock.

number of stock, and season of use for the area will be determined by
agreement .between Rex Gardner and The Bureau of Land Management. If agreement
cannot be reached final decision will be made by the District Manager.

Objectives:
The short-term objective for the project area would be to reduce the shrub canopy to
less than 20 percent. The mid-term objective would be to increase the percent canopy cover of
desired grasses and forbs, to at least twice that of the control plot percentages within five years of
treatment. The long-term, landscape-scale objective would be to maintain a sagebrush, grass and
forb community so that there are ample amounts of all the sagebrush cover classes in a mosaic
across the landscape as identified for sage grouse and other sagebrush obligates (Connelly et al.
2000).
Planned_Implementation:
The proposed action is to rotomow 40 percent (\xb1 10 percent) of the identified 1,336 acres of
crested wheatgrass seeding with moderately dense (23 percent cover) Wyoming sagebrush
(Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis) habitat that is considered to be in poor health and in a
less than desirable ecological condition (Figure 2). The shrub canopy will be mowed by the
above stated percent leaving untouched shrub patches or strips that will act as sources for
sagebrush seed dispersion while maintaining sufficient habitat for wildlife species. Mow height
will be preset at eight inches prior to project initiation. The preset mow height will allow for
many sagebrush seedlings present in the project area to be unaffected by the proposed
implementation. All hydrologic features identified will be buffered by at least 50 feet and
avoided so as to reduce any increased sediment loading and/or bank erosion.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The purpose of the proposed action is to restore sagebrush-steppe habitat in the lowlands of the
Sheep Mountain and Alder Creek allotments in Custer County (Figure 1) to a suitable condition
as sage grouse breeding habitat. The proposed action is needed to improve a native plant
community and provide a diversity of plant species and structure needed to meet BLM&$s public
land management obligations and mandates. These mandates include restoring rangeland health,
implementing BLM&$s National Sage-Grouse Habitat Conservation Strategy, the Upper Snake
Sage Grouse Local Working Group Plan, the National Fire Plan, and meeting resource objectives
stated in the Big Lost Management Framework Plan (BLMFP) (December 1983). The proposed
action is needed in the Sheep Mountain project area in order to increase native plant and animal
diversity and reduce the potential for large wildfires that could threaten surrounding private
property.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: Conifer trees use more water through transpiration than aspen and have sparse undergrowth with relatively few species (Bartos and Campbell 1998). Bartos and Campbell (1998) suggest this displacement could cause the annual forfeiture of 375,000 acre feet of water that would have been available for steam flow and annual loss of 750,000 tons of biomass production in the mountains of Utah. Planned_Implementation:
Machine piles shall be reasonably compact and free of soil to facilitate burning. Piles will be at
least 10 feet in height. Piles shall be of a size and location which will not impair road use or result in damage to
residual timber. Piles shall be located at least 50 feet from residual timber. Piles shall not be more than 10 feet
long. All objects which extend more than 4 feet in any direction from the windrow or pile profile will be cut off and
returned to the windrow or pile.
Hand Piling: All slash 9 inches diameter at breast height and less shall be piled. This includes any downed and dead material already on 
the ground. All slash in deciduous stands shall be piled. This includes any downed and dead material already on
the ground. All piles shall be constructed by laying limbs, stems, cut boles, and other slash in the pile
triangular or domed in shape. Slash that causes large air spaces in piles shall be cut to eliminate air spaces. Each pile
shall include an area of small sized slash (small branches less than 1/4 to 1/2 inch in diameter and/or small branches
with needles or leaves attached) to provide "kindling" for prompt ignition and to aid in combustion of larger slash.
These fuels shall be placed in the center of the pile. 1
Unless approved by the COR, maximum pile size shall be 8 feet in diameter and 10 feet in height, and minimum pile
size shall be 5 feet in diameter by 7 feet in height.
Piles shall not be closer than 10 feet to live trees or 25 feet to a unit boundary 
unless approved by the COR. Slash shall not be piled or placed on roads or trails,
or drainage ditches, or... within channel bottoms or streams. Slash shall not be piled within 25 feet of the area directly
under a power line. Piles will not be covered.

Planned_Implementation:
Implement the use of Integrated Pest Management (IPM). IPM applies multiple methods
where practicable. These methods would be applied within various salt cedar and
Russian olive infested habitats. Majority of the weed treatments would be applied on
public lands and would include small acreages of private lands adjacent to public lands.
Treatments would be applied throughout the year, during optimal period of treatments.
This alternative would combine all of the treatment options available. Primary treatment
methodologies would include (1) cutting salt cedar and Russian olive trees and shrubs to
a height of approximately 16" inches above ground and immediately applying herbicide
to the cut stumps; (2) use of targeted low volume basal application of herbicide to small
diameter trees/shrubs, (3) mechanical removal of dense stands, and ( 4) use of biological
control vectors when they become available in the future.

IPM methods would include educating staff, cooperators, and the public in prevention,
early detection and rapid response to all noxious and select invasive plant species. Also,
continued inventory of public lands for noxious and invasive plants, control of noxious
and invasive plants by various methods that include cultural, physical, biological, and
chemical controls or other land practices, and monitor treatment areas.

The following actions would be employed solely or in combination at infested sites:
Pre-treatment where needed:
1. Prescribed fire would be utilized to clear the area of decadent vegetation and to
improve the efficacy of the applied treatments.
2. Mechanical removal of undergrowth would be utilized to facilitate access for
removal operations.

Treatment options include:
1. Mechanical felling of target species, to include: hand removal, chainsaw, tractor
implement, brush hawg.
2. Pesticide application for Russian olive and salt cedar, including the following
active ingredients: Triclopyr, (e.g. Garland 3A\xae, Remedy\xae, Tahoe 3A\xae),
Glyphosate (e.g. Rodeo\xae, Aquamaster\xae, Roundup PRO\xae). Follow up
treatments to prevent reinfestation of other noxious species would include the
following active ingredients Triclopyr (e.g. Habitat\xae, Garland 3A\xae, Remedy\xae,
Tahoe 3A\xae), Glyphosate (e.g. Rodeo\xae, Aquamaster\xae, Roundup PRO\xae) and
2,4-D (e.g. Weedar 64\xae).
3. Combination of treatments 1 and 2, where the vegetation is removed
mechanically and the exposed stumps are chemically treated to prevent resprouts.
4. Girdling and chemically treated to prevent re-sprouts of larger trees with follow
up mechanical removal.

Disposal options include:
1. Pile and burn on site.
2. Haul away to an approved landfill.
3. Chipped and scattered on site.
4. Left in place to act as a protective barrier for post treatment seedlings.
5. Large material could be bucked and used in recreation sites for fire wood.
6. On site incineration.

Post Treatment Management options include:
1. Seed bed preparation, including: discing, harrowing, and hand preparation.
2. Reseed with native species (broadcast, hydromulch, hand rake, drill)
3. Use of root stock or plugs to re-establish native woody shrubs and trees.
4. Allow natural recruitment where the native community allows.
5. Transplant native woody species from onsite, adjacent public lands, or from
nursenes.
Best Management Practices (BMPs );
• Post treatment monitoring of revegetation success and to detect re-colonization of
noxious species.
• Cultural inventories of all sites where ground disturbing activities would occur prior to
commencing work.
• Implementation would occur throughout the year. Cut stump application on salt cedar
and Russian olive would occur throughout the year during optimum weather conditions.
• See Appendix A for a list of other SOPs.
Salt cedar would be treated with a foliar spray of herbicide applied by ground based
equipment. Triclopyr would be used as a basal bark or cut stump treatment. Treatment
applications would be made primarily by backpack, pickup truck, or ATV mounted spray
equipment. Backpack application is more precise type of application to target Russian
olive and salt cedar plants. Maintenance treatments would also generally be restricted to
the use of ground spray equipment.

Mitigation Measures/Remarks
1. Herbicide application will conform to procedures found in BLM Handbook H-9011-1,
and the Herbicide Label.
2. An approved Pesticide Use Proposal will be obtained prior to herbicide use.
3. All trash and unused materials will be removed and properly disposed of upon
completion of the project.
4. Off-road driving will be kept to a minimum and limited to dry ground, dry weather
conditions.
5. A cultural survey must be conducted prior to any manual or mechanical treatments, or the use of prescribed fire.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Control noxious and invasive woody species through a variety of control methods. In particular,
Russian olive (Elaeagnus angustifolia) and salt cedar (Tamarix ramosissima) would be
targeted in riparian areas, to assist with the attainment of Proper Functioning Condition
Standards, and to maintain native riparian communities that are healthy.

The purpose for the proposed project is to restore native riparian habitat by treating salt
cedar and Russian olive using principals of lntegrated Weed Management (IWM). Areas
targeted for treatments would be along stream zones or riparian areas on public land
administered by the Billings Field Office with an emphasis on larger acreages of
invasion. Monitoring and treatments of herbaceous noxious weeds would also occur to
prevent the introduction and spread.

The Bureau is required by specific authorities to manage invasive/noxious weeds. The
Need is to prevent the spread and further invasion of Russian olive and salt cedar.
Salt Cedar, a federally and state listed noxious weed, and Russian olive, an invasive
species, are infesting various watersheds within the Billings Field Office area.

The invasion of native plant communities by noxious and invasive plant species is a continuous threat in Montana with ecological and economic consequences. Noxious and invasive weeds spread in many ways: animals (livestock,
birds, or other wildlife), pets, people hiking, bicycling, and all forms of motorized
equipment, movement down streams, wind, etc. By implementing IWM, existing
populations of noxious and invasive plants would be contained to the extent practicable.
New invasive species would be identified early and eradicated or contained through Early
Detection and Rapid Response.

Riparian vegetation provides in-stream habitat for fish, adds structure to the banks,
reduces erosion, moderates water temperatures, and is a source of organic nutrients for
the system. Riparian vegetation moderates flows by reducing runoff to the stream and
stores water for later release. As riparian habitats degrade, erosion and sedimentation increase and streams widen and become shallower. Temperature fluctuations increase and oxygen content could reach critically low levels.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Crested wheatgrass is an introduced species that has very high potential as
early season forage for livestock. However, crested wheatgrass has to be
managed closely to keep a pasture as productive as possible. Over a long
period of time an improperly managed crested wheatgrass pasture will show a
characteristic pattern of dense bunches of rank crested wheatgrass plants
intermingled with areas of clubmoss or low vigor blue grama. Range productivity
in this situation is considerably lower than a good condition, well managed
crested wheatgrass pasture. Such a situation exists in Pasture 4 of the Halfway
Coulee Allotment. It is estimated that this pasture is currently producing
about half of the recognized carrying capacity.

Actual_Implementation: One the second time over (plow) they attached a rotary type broadcaster behind the harrows and followed these with till and pack type toothed cultipackers.
